hints.text: What is a spanning tree, and how many edges must one have when the graph has four vertices?
A tree is connected and has no cycle, so with $n$ vertices it has exactly $n-1$ edges. A spanning tree uses every vertex of the graph.
The vertices are labelled, so two trees with the same shape but different labels are different spanning trees. There is a classical formula that counts labelled trees on $n$ vertices.
Either apply that formula with $n = 4$, or count by shape: list the shapes a tree on four vertices can have and count the labellings of each shape.
Start with the shape in which one vertex is joined to all the other three. How many choices are there for the centre?

variation.stem: The number of spanning trees in a complete graph of 6 vertices labelled A, B, C, D, E and F is ______
variation.explanation: Spanning trees of the complete graph on $n$ labelled vertices number $n^{n-2}$. With $n = 6$ this is $6^4 = 1296$. A determinant computation from the matrix-tree theorem on the Laplacian of $K_6$ gives the same value.

questions.stem: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. Let $G$ be any graph with $n$ vertices and chromatic number $k$. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
options: $G$ contains a complete subgraph with $k$ vertices
$G$ contains an independent set of size at least $n/k$
$G$ contains a vertex of degree at least $k$

solutionDiagram.alt: Two counterexamples: a 5-cycle coloured 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, which needs 3 colours yet has no triangle, and the complete graph on 4 vertices, which needs 4 colours yet every vertex has degree 3.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A **proper colouring** gives different colours to the two ends of every edge. The **chromatic number** $k$ is the fewest colours that make a proper colouring possible. A **colour class** is the set of vertices that received one colour; no two of them are adjacent, so a colour class is an **independent set**. A **complete subgraph** on $k$ vertices (a clique) has all its $k$ vertices pairwise adjacent. "Always true" means true for every graph with these properties: one graph where a statement fails removes it, and the true ones need a proof.

steps.title: B is true: pigeonhole on colour classes
steps.body: An optimal colouring splits the $n$ vertices into $k$ colour classes. If every class had fewer than $n/k$ vertices, the total would be less than $k \cdot n/k = n$. So some class has at least $n/k$ vertices, and that class is an independent set.

steps.title: C is true: every two classes are joined by an edge
steps.body: Take an optimal colouring with classes $C_1, \dots, C_k$. If no edge joined $C_i$ to $C_j$, the two classes could be merged into one and still be proper, giving a colouring with $k-1$ colours and contradicting the minimality of $k$. So every one of the $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs of classes is joined by at least one edge, and one edge serves only one pair. The graph has at least $k(k-1)/2$ edges.

steps.title: A and D fail
steps.body: For A take the 5-cycle: an odd cycle cannot be coloured with 2 colours, so $k = 3$, yet it has no triangle. For D take the complete graph $K_k$: it needs $k$ colours and every vertex has degree $k-1$, which is less than $k$. A brute-force search over all graphs on up to 6 vertices finds counterexamples to A and D and none to B and C. The answer is B and C.

shortcut.body: Try two small graphs: the 5-cycle kills A (3 colours, no triangle) and $K_k$ kills D (degree $k-1$). For B and C recall the proofs, which are one line each: pigeonhole on the $k$ classes, and "two classes with no edge between them could be merged". About 2 minutes. Testing graphs can only eliminate a statement, never prove it.

traps.text: Option A is the clique-number idea: it holds when $\chi$ equals the clique number (perfect graphs), but not in general. The 5-cycle has $k = 3$ and no triangle.
Option B is easy to skip because $n/k$ looks unfamiliar. It is only the average class size, and the largest class is at least the average.
Option C is true even though it looks too strong: with $k = 4$ it asks for 6 edges, and $K_4$ has exactly 6. The edge between every two colour classes is forced by minimality.
Option D confuses degree with colours: a $k$-chromatic graph always has a vertex of degree at least $k-1$, not $k$. $K_k$ has all degrees equal to $k-1$.

recognize.clues: "Always true" about a graph with $n$ vertices and chromatic number $k$ is a general statement about colour classes. The quantities named are cliques, independent sets, edge counts and degrees, all tied to $k$.
recognize.contrast: The chromatic number is at least the clique size but can be larger, so a clique of size $k$ is not guaranteed. Do not mix the lower bound $k \ge \omega(G)$ with the false converse.

check.body: Test all four statements on the 5-cycle ($n=5$, $k=3$) and on the complete graph $K_4$. The cycle has independent sets of size 2, at least $5/3$, and has 5 edges, at least $3$, but no triangle and maximum degree 2. $K_4$ has $k=4$, 6 edges (at least 6) and degree 3 everywhere. The statements that survive both graphs are the only candidates, and the proofs from the colour classes show they hold in general.

hints.text: For each statement, ask whether you can prove it for every graph or find one graph that breaks it. Which of the four look provable and which look breakable?
A colour class is a set of vertices sharing one colour, so no two of them are adjacent. Every proper colouring cuts the vertex set into such independent classes.
Whatever statement you test, either prove it for all graphs from the colour classes of an optimal colouring, or break it with a small graph whose chromatic number you know.
To test by example, record for a graph its chromatic number, its largest complete subgraph, its edge count and its degrees. To test by proof, start from the colour classes of an optimal colouring.
Take the 5-cycle: work out its chromatic number, whether it has a triangle, its number of edges and its vertex degrees. Compare each with the four statements.

variation.stem: Suppose a graph on $n$ vertices needs exactly $k$ colours in a proper colouring. Which of the following must hold, whatever the graph is?
options: $G$ has a vertex of degree at least $k - 1$
If $k \ge 3$, then $G$ contains a cycle of odd length
In every proper colouring of $G$ with $k$ colours, each colour class has exactly $n/k$ vertices
variation.explanation: A graph that needs $k$ colours contains a subgraph in which every vertex has degree at least $k-1$, so a vertex of degree $k-1$ always exists. A graph with no odd cycle can be split into two groups, so $k \ge 3$ forces an odd cycle. The 5-cycle has $k = 3$ and no triangle, and the path on three vertices has $k = 2$ but colour classes of sizes 2 and 1. A search over all graphs with up to 6 vertices found no counterexample to the first two and counterexamples to the last two.

questions.stem: Consider the operators $\lozenge$ and $\square$ defined by $a \lozenge b = a + 2b$, $a \square b = ab$, for positive integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: Operator $\lozenge$ over the operator $\square$ obeys the distributive law
Operator $\square$ over the operator $\lozenge$ obeys the distributive law

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: An operation $\circ$ is **associative** when $(a \circ b) \circ c = a \circ (b \circ c)$ for all values: the grouping does not matter. Operation $\circ$ **distributes over** operation $*$ when $a \circ (b * c) = (a \circ b) * (a \circ c)$, and, when $\circ$ is not commutative, also $(b * c) \circ a = (b \circ a) * (c \circ a)$. To prove a law you must show it for all positive integers; to disprove it, one example is enough.

steps.title: Associativity of the two operators
steps.body: Expand both groupings of $\lozenge$: $(a \lozenge b) \lozenge c = (a + 2b) + 2c = a + 2b + 2c$, while $a \lozenge (b \lozenge c) = a + 2(b + 2c) = a + 2b + 4c$. They differ whenever $c \ne 0$; for $a = b = c = 1$ they are 5 and 7. So A is false. $\square$ is ordinary multiplication, and $(ab)c = a(bc)$, so B is true.
steps.tex: (a \lozenge b) \lozenge c = a + 2b + 2c \ \ne\ a + 2b + 4c = a \lozenge (b \lozenge c)

steps.title: Distributivity in both directions
steps.body: "$\lozenge$ over $\square$" asks whether $a \lozenge (b \square c) = (a \lozenge b) \square (a \lozenge c)$. The left side is $a + 2bc$, the right side is $(a + 2b)(a + 2c) = a^2 + 2ac + 2ab + 4bc$; for $a = b = c = 1$ they are 3 and 9. So C is false. "$\square$ over $\lozenge$" asks whether $a(b + 2c) = ab + 2ac$, which is $(a \square b) \lozenge (a \square c)$, and it is true. The mirror form $(b + 2c)a = ba + 2ca$ holds too. So D is true. The answer is B and D, which a brute-force check of all triples up to 7 confirms.
steps.tex: a \square (b \lozenge c) = a(b + 2c) = ab + 2ac = (a \square b) \lozenge (a \square c)

shortcut.body: Plug in $a = b = c = 1$: $\lozenge$ associativity gives 5 against 7, and $\lozenge$ over $\square$ gives 3 against 9, so A and C die in 30 seconds. B is multiplication, and D is the ordinary law $a(b + 2c) = ab + 2ac$. Numbers can only disprove a law, so B and D must be recognised by algebra, not by testing.

traps.text: Option A: $a + 2b$ looks like addition, which is associative, but the factor 2 on the second argument makes the left and right groupings weigh $c$ differently (2 against 4).
Option C reverses the familiar law. "$\lozenge$ over $\square$" is addition-over-multiplication, which fails even for plain numbers: $a + bc \ne (a + b)(a + c)$.
Option D is rejected by candidates who note that $\lozenge$ is not commutative. Both the left and the right distributive forms hold, so nothing is lost.

recognize.clues: Two operators are defined by formulas on positive integers, and the options ask about associativity and distributivity. That is the test for algebraic laws of an operation, answered by expanding both sides.
recognize.contrast: A binary operation can be commutative without being associative. Associativity concerns grouping, distributivity involves two operations and an order of application, so do not swap their roles.

check.body: Substitute fresh numbers, $a = 2$, $b = 3$, $c = 4$. Multiplication: $(2\cdot3)\cdot4 = 24 = 2\cdot(3\cdot4)$. The distributive form of $\square$ over $\lozenge$: $2(3 + 2\cdot4) = 22$ and $2\cdot3 + 2\cdot(2\cdot4) = 22$. These agree with the algebra, though numbers alone could never prove them. The two failing laws fail at these numbers too: $\lozenge$ gives 16 and 24 for the two groupings.

hints.text: Each option states a law about an operator. Which of the laws can you test with a quick numerical example, and which can only be settled by algebra?

Associative means the grouping of three values does not change the result. Distributive means one operation spreads over the other, and when the operation is not symmetric both sides need to be checked.
One counterexample kills a law, but no number of examples proves it. To confirm a law that survives testing, expand both sides symbolically and compare.

For the associativity options write out $(a \circ b) \circ c$ and $a \circ (b \circ c)$ using the given definition. For the distributive options write the left and right sides with the definitions substituted, then simplify each.
For the first operator, expand $(a \lozenge b) \lozenge c$ by replacing $a \lozenge b$ with $a + 2b$ first. Then expand the other grouping and compare the coefficient of $c$.

variation.stem: Consider the operators $\ast$, $\oplus$ and $\otimes$ defined on positive integers by $a \ast b = 2a + b$, $a \oplus b = \max(a, b)$ and $a \otimes b = a + b$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: Operator $\otimes$ over the operator $\oplus$ obeys the distributive law
Operator $\oplus$ over the operator $\otimes$ obeys the distributive law
variation.explanation: For $\ast$ the groupings give $4a + 2b + c$ and $2a + 2b + c$, which differ. The maximum of three numbers does not depend on grouping, so $\oplus$ is associative. Adding a number to a maximum equals the maximum of the sums, so $\otimes$ distributes over $\oplus$. In the other direction $\max(a, b + c)$ is not $\max(a,b) + \max(a,c)$: for $a = 5$, $b = c = 1$ the values are 5 and 10. Checked by running all triples up to 8.

questions.stem: The Lucas sequence $L_n$ is defined by the recurrence relation: $L_n = L_{n-1} + L_{n-2}$, for $n \ge 3$, with $L_1 = 1$ and $L_2 = 3$. Which one of the options given is TRUE?

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A **recurrence** gives each term from earlier ones; here every term is the sum of the previous two, starting from $L_1 = 1$ and $L_2 = 3$, so the sequence runs $1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, \dots$. A **closed form** is a formula in $n$ alone. A closed form is correct when it matches the starting values and obeys the recurrence. Trying $L_n = r^n$ in $L_n = L_{n-1} + L_{n-2}$ gives $r^2 = r + 1$, whose roots are $\varphi = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ and $\psi = \frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}$, so every solution has the form $\alpha\varphi^n + \beta\psi^n$.

steps.title: Use the two sums of roots
steps.body: The roots satisfy $\varphi + \psi = 1$ and $\varphi\psi = -1$. Then $\varphi^2 + \psi^2 = (\varphi + \psi)^2 - 2\varphi\psi = 1 + 2 = 3$. So $\varphi^n + \psi^n$ equals 1 for $n = 1$ and 3 for $n = 2$: exactly $L_1$ and $L_2$. Because $\varphi^n + \psi^n$ also obeys the recurrence (each power does), it equals $L_n$ for all $n$. Option A is correct.

steps.title: The other options fail at n = 1
steps.body: B at $n = 1$: $\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} - \frac{1-\sqrt5}{3} \approx 2.03$. C at $n = 1$: $\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} + \frac{1-\sqrt5}{3} \approx 1.21$. D at $n = 1$: $\varphi - \psi = \sqrt5 \approx 2.24$. None equals $L_1 = 1$. A numerical check of all four options over $n = 1, \dots, 11$ agrees: only A matches the sequence.

shortcut.body: Put $n = 1$ and require the value 1. Only A gives it, because $\varphi + \psi = 1$ (the sum of the roots of $r^2 - r - 1$). Thirty seconds, and safe here because the four options differ already at $n = 1$.

traps.text: Option B has a denominator 3 in the second base and a minus sign. The number $\frac{1-\sqrt5}{3}$ is not a root of $r^2 = r + 1$, so its powers do not obey the recurrence, and B already fails at $n = 1$: it gives about 2.03 instead of $L_1 = 1$.
Option C is the same slip as B with a plus sign: the second base must be the other root $\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}$, not $\frac{1-\sqrt5}{3}$.

Option D is the Fibonacci pattern without the division by $\sqrt5$: $\varphi^n - \psi^n$ equals $\sqrt5\,F_n$, not $L_n$. Lucas numbers add the two powers, and Fibonacci numbers subtract them and divide.

recognize.clues: A linear recurrence with constant coefficients and two starting values is given, and the options are formulas in $n$. That means checking a closed form against the characteristic roots and starting values.
recognize.contrast: This is not a generating-function problem even though the sequence is Fibonacci-like. It is the same recurrence as Fibonacci but with different starting values, so the Fibonacci closed form with a minus sign (which gives $\sqrt5$) is the look-alike to avoid.

check.body: Compute the next term from the recurrence, $L_3 = L_2 + L_1 = 4$. Using $\varphi + \psi = 1$ and $\varphi\psi = -1$, $\varphi^3 + \psi^3 = (\varphi + \psi)^3 - 3\varphi\psi(\varphi + \psi) = 1 + 3 = 4$. A term the closed form was not fitted to also matches.

hints.text: The options are closed forms. What must be true of a correct closed form at the starting values of the sequence?
A recurrence with two starting values fixes the whole sequence. A closed form is right when it reproduces the starting values and satisfies the same recurrence.

Trying $r^n$ in a recurrence that adds the previous two terms gives the quadratic $r^2 = r + 1$. The two roots are the bases that appear in every solution, so only a combination of those two powers can be correct.
Do not solve for the constants. Instead test each option at $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ against the given starting values $L_1 = 1$ and $L_2 = 3$.
Let the two roots be $\varphi$ and $\psi$. Their sum and product come from the quadratic. Work out what $\varphi^n + \psi^n$ and $\varphi^n - \psi^n$ give at $n = 1$ and compare with $L_1 = 1$.

variation.stem: The sequence $a_n$ is defined by $a_n = a_{n-1} + 2a_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 3$, with $a_1 = 1$ and $a_2 = 5$. Which one of the options given is TRUE?
variation.explanation: The characteristic equation $r^2 = r + 2$ has roots 2 and $-1$, so $a_n = \alpha 2^n + \beta(-1)^n$. The values $a_1 = 1$ and $a_2 = 5$ give $\alpha = \beta = 1$. At $n = 1$ option A gives 3, option C gives 0 and option D gives 2, so only B matches. The terms $1, 5, 7, 17, 31, 65$ agree with B for $n$ up to 12.

questions.stem: Geetha has a conjecture about integers, which is of the form $\forall x \left( P(x) \implies \exists y\, Q(x, y) \right)$, where $P$ is a statement about integers, and $Q$ is a statement about pairs of integers. Which of the following (one or more) option(s) would imply Geetha's conjecture?

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: $P(x)$ and $Q(x, y)$ are predicates: statements that become true or false once values are put in. $\forall x$ reads "for every $x$" and $\exists y$ reads "there is at least one $y$". An implication $R \implies S$ is false only when $R$ is true and $S$ is false. Geetha's conjecture says: every $x$ with $P(x)$ true has at least one partner $y$ with $Q(x, y)$ true. An option **implies** the conjecture when the conjecture is true in every situation where the option is true; to show an option does not imply it, find one situation where the option is true and the conjecture is false.

steps.title: B implies it
steps.body: Option B says $Q(x, y)$ holds for every pair. Then for any $x$ and any $y$ at all, $Q(x, y)$ is true, so $\exists y\, Q(x, y)$ is true for every $x$ (there is at least one integer to use as $y$). The implication $P(x) \implies \exists y\, Q(x, y)$ then has a true right-hand side for every $x$, so it is true for every $x$.

steps.title: C implies it
steps.body: Option C says there is one fixed $y_0$ such that for every $x$, $P(x) \implies Q(x, y_0)$. Take any $x$ with $P(x)$ true; then $Q(x, y_0)$ is true, so $x$ has the partner $y_0$. That is exactly the conjecture. Moving $\exists y$ in front of $\forall x$ made the statement stronger, because one $y_0$ now serves all $x$.
steps.tex: \exists y\, \forall x\, (P(x) \implies Q(x, y)) \ \Longrightarrow\ \forall x\, (P(x) \implies \exists y\, Q(x, y))

steps.title: A and D do not imply it
steps.body: Both begin with $\exists x$: they speak about one $x$ only. Take two integers 1 and 2, with $P$ true for both. Let $Q(1, y)$ be true for every $y$ and $Q(2, y)$ false for every $y$. Then A is true (with $x = 1$, $P(1)$ holds and $Q(1, y)$ holds for all $y$) and D is true, but the conjecture fails at $x = 2$. An exhaustive check over all interpretations on 1, 2 and 3 elements agrees: B and C never leave the conjecture false, and A and D do. The answer is B and C.

shortcut.body: The conjecture speaks about every $x$; A and D start with $\exists x$ and speak about one, so they cannot imply it. B is plainly stronger, since $Q$ holds everywhere. For C, one $y$ working for all $x$ is stronger than a $y$ for each $x$. About a minute and a half.

traps.text: Option A looks strong because of the $\forall y$ inside, but the outer $\exists x$ covers a single $x$. Any other $x$ with $P(x)$ true can still lack a partner.

Option C is left out by candidates who see the swapped quantifiers and judge it "a different statement". Swapping $\forall x \exists y$ to $\exists y \forall x$ only strengthens it, and a stronger statement still implies the weaker one.

Option D starts with $\exists x$, so it speaks about one $x$ only, while the conjecture needs a partner for every $x$ with $P(x)$ true. D holds in the counterexample of step 4 ($P$ true for 1 and 2, $Q(1, y)$ true for all $y$, $Q(2, y)$ false for all $y$) although the conjecture fails at $x = 2$.

recognize.clues: The question asks which statements imply a given universally quantified conjecture, so it is about logical consequence in first-order logic, decided by quantifier order and by looking for a counter-model.
recognize.contrast: This is not translation of an English sentence into a formula. Here nothing is read from words; the test is implication, settled by a proof or a small counter-model.

check.body: Check one of the surviving options by contradiction. Suppose the conjecture fails: some $x_0$ has $P(x_0)$ true and $Q(x_0, y)$ false for every $y$. If the option claims a single $y_0$ with $P(x) \implies Q(x, y_0)$ for all $x$, then at $x_0$ it demands $Q(x_0, y_0)$, which is false, a contradiction. So that option cannot be true while the conjecture fails.

hints.text: The conjecture says every $x$ with $P(x)$ has a partner $y$. What would you need to know about an option for it to guarantee that for all such $x$?
To imply a statement, an option must make it true in every situation where the option is true. One situation where the option holds and the conjecture fails is enough to rule the option out.
Quantifier order matters. Compare where each quantifier sits in an option with where it sits in the conjecture, and ask whether the option covers every $x$ that satisfies $P$ or only some.
For each option, either argue directly that the conjecture follows, or build a small situation where the option is true but some $x$ with $P(x)$ has no partner.
Suppose the conjecture fails at some $x_0$. What must be true of $P(x_0)$, and of $Q(x_0, y)$ for every $y$? Then see which options that situation contradicts.

variation.stem: A student conjectures $\forall x \left( P(x) \implies \exists y\, R(x, y) \right)$ over a non-empty domain. Which of the following (one or more) would imply the conjecture?
variation.explanation: Option A gives one $y_0$ that works for every $x$ with $P(x)$, which is stronger than the conjecture. Option B says each $x$ satisfies $P$ and has a partner, so the conjecture holds. Option C speaks about one $x$ and can leave another $x$ without a partner. Option D can hold while an $x$ with $P(x)$ has no partner, for example when the domain is $\{1,2\}$, $P$ is true of both, $R(1, y)$ is true for all $y$ and $R(2, y)$ is false for all $y$. An exhaustive check over all interpretations on up to 3 elements agrees.

questions.stem:
Let $U = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, where $n$ is a large positive integer greater than 1000. Let $k$ be a positive integer less than $n$. Let $A, B$ be subsets of $U$ with $|A| = |B| = k$ and $A \cap B = \emptyset$. We say that a permutation of $U$ separates $A$ from $B$ if one of the following is true.

- All members of $A$ appear in the permutation before any of the members of $B$.
- All members of $B$ appear in the permutation before any of the members of $A$.

How many permutations of $U$ separate $A$ from $B$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two rows of nine cells for n = 9 and k = 2. In the first row the first two chosen cells hold A and the last two hold B; in the second row the roles are swapped. The other five cells are marked with a dot. The product formula 2 times C(n, 2k) times (k!)^2 times (n - 2k)! is written below.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A **permutation** of $U$ lists all $n$ elements once each in some order, so there are $n!$ permutations. $\binom{n}{r}$ is the number of ways to choose which $r$ of $n$ places are used. A permutation **separates** $A$ from $B$ when the whole block of $A$ comes before the whole block of $B$ or the other way round, with other elements allowed anywhere. The rule is the multiplication principle: when a count is built by independent choices made one after another, multiply the number of options of each choice.

steps.title: Choose the places of A and B
steps.body: The $2k$ members of $A \cup B$ take up $2k$ of the $n$ places in the list. Choosing which places they occupy can be done in $\binom{n}{2k}$ ways.

steps.title: Decide who goes first and fill the places
steps.body: Read the chosen places from left to right. Either the first $k$ of them belong to $A$ and the last $k$ to $B$, or the other way round: 2 choices. Inside the $k$ places of $A$ the members of $A$ can be arranged in $k!$ ways, and likewise $k!$ for $B$. The remaining $n - 2k$ elements fill the remaining places in $(n-2k)!$ ways.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: The total is the product of the four independent choices. It matches option D. A brute-force count agrees: for $n = 5$, $k = 2$ the count is 40, and $2\binom{5}{4}\cdot 1! \cdot (2!)^2 = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 = 40$; for $n = 7$, $k = 3$ both give 504.

shortcut.body: Take the smallest case with room to separate: $n = 4$, $k = 2$, so $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{3, 4\}$. The blocks $AB$ and $BA$ each have $2! \cdot 2! = 4$ orders, total 8. Option A gives 24, B gives 1, C gives 4, D gives 8. Only D matches. One test case decides it because the four formulas already differ there.

traps.text: $n!$ counts every permutation, as if separation were automatic. For $n = 4$, $k = 2$ most of the 24 orders mix $A$ and $B$.
Choosing the places and filling the other elements, but forgetting that $A$ and $B$ can be ordered inside their own places ($k!$ each) and who goes first.
Option C counts only "$A$ before $B$". The question allows the mirror case, "$B$ before $A$", so the count doubles.

recognize.clues: The wording asks for a number of permutations under a block condition on two disjoint subsets of equal size $k$, with the rest of $U$ unrestricted. That calls for choosing positions, then arranging inside the blocks.
recognize.contrast: Do not treat it as a count of orderings of only $2k$ items: the other $n - 2k$ elements also move, and the positions of $A \cup B$ are not fixed. Fixing them would give the wrong binomial factor.

check.body: Second route by symmetry. Among the $(2k)!$ equally likely relative orders of the $2k$ special elements, exactly $2(k!)^2$ put all of one set before all of the other. So the count is $n!$ times $2(k!)^2/(2k)!$, which equals $2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2$ because $\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)! = n!/(2k)!$.

hints.text: Ask what the condition forces about the positions of the $2k$ special elements, and what it leaves free for everyone else.
Counting a permutation can be split into independent choices: where some elements sit, then how they are ordered, then how the rest fill in.
Multiply the number of options of each independent choice. Choosing $r$ places out of $n$ is a binomial coefficient, and arranging $m$ labelled items is $m!$.
Choose the places taken by $A \cup B$ first. Reading those places left to right, ask which sets can fill the first $k$ of them, then ask how each block is internally ordered.
Test your formula on $n = 4$, $k = 2$ by listing the permutations of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ that put $\{1,2\}$ wholly before or wholly after $\{3,4\}$, and compare with each option.

variation.stem: Let $U = \{1, 2, \ldots, 6\}$ and let $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{3, 4\}$. A permutation of $U$ separates $A$ from $B$ if all of $A$ appears before all of $B$ or all of $B$ appears before all of $A$. How many permutations of $U$ separate $A$ from $B$?
variation.explanation: Choose the 4 places for $A \cup B$ in $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ ways, pick which set comes first (2 ways), order each block ($2! \cdot 2! = 4$), and fill the other 2 places in $2! = 2$ ways: $15 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 = 240$. Dropping the factor 2 gives 120, dropping the block orderings gives 60, and 720 counts every permutation.

questions.stem: Let $f : A \to B$ be an onto (or surjective) function, where $A$ and $B$ are nonempty sets. Define an equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A$ as $a_1 \sim a_2$ if $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$, where $a_1, a_2 \in A$. Let $\mathcal{E} = \{[x] : x \in A\}$ be the set of all the equivalence classes under $\sim$. Define a new mapping $F : \mathcal{E} \to B$ as $F([x]) = f(x)$, for all the equivalence classes $[x]$ in $\mathcal{E}$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: Example with A = {1,...,6} and B = {x, y, z}: the six elements of A are grouped by arrows into three classes [1] = {1,2}, [3] = {3} and [4] = {4,5,6}, and each class has one arrow to a different element of B, which is the map F.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: An **equivalence class** $[x]$ is the set of all elements related to $x$. Here $a_1 \sim a_2$ means $f$ sends them to the same output, so each class is the set of inputs that land on one output value. $F$ sends a class to that common value. **Well-defined** means the rule gives one answer however the class is named: if $[x] = [y]$ then $F([x])$ and $F([y])$ must agree. **Onto** means every element of $B$ is hit. **One-to-one** means different classes give different outputs. **Bijective** means both.

steps.title: F is well-defined, so A is false
steps.body: If $[x] = [y]$ then $x \sim y$, which by the definition of $\sim$ says $f(x) = f(y)$. So $F([x]) = f(x) = f(y) = F([y])$: the value does not depend on the representative.

steps.title: F is onto
steps.body: Take any $b \in B$. Because $f$ is onto there is some $a \in A$ with $f(a) = b$. Then $F([a]) = f(a) = b$, so $b$ is hit.

steps.title: F is one-to-one, hence bijective
steps.body: Suppose $F([x]) = F([y])$. Then $f(x) = f(y)$, so $x \sim y$, so $[x] = [y]$. Different classes therefore have different outputs. Being onto and one-to-one, $F$ is bijective. True statements: B, C, D. A random search over 2000 surjections on small sets found $F$ always well-defined, onto and one-to-one.

shortcut.body: This is the standard factorisation $f = F \circ (\text{class map})$: collapsing inputs that $f$ already identifies makes $F$ one-to-one, and $f$ onto makes $F$ onto. So B, C and D are true and A is false. A minute, because the relation was built from $f$ itself.

traps.text: Option A is tempting because maps defined on classes are often ill-defined, for example $[x] \mapsto x$. Here the relation is built from $f$, so the value cannot depend on the representative.
Option C is rejected by candidates who note that $f$ itself need not be one-to-one. That is the point of the construction: the classes absorb exactly the collisions of $f$.
Stopping after B and C leaves out D. A function that is onto and one-to-one is bijective by definition.

recognize.clues: The relation is defined from $f$ itself, and a new map $F$ is defined on classes by a representative. That is the pattern of a map induced on a quotient, which asks for well-definedness, onto and one-to-one.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse the classes with the points of $A$. $F$ acts on classes, so one-to-one means distinct classes, not distinct elements of $A$, and $f$ itself is usually not one-to-one.

check.body: Count check on a finite case. The classes are exactly the fibres $f^{-1}(b)$, one for each $b \in B$ because $f$ is onto, so $|\mathcal{E}| = |B|$. A map between two finite sets of equal size that hits every element must also be one-to-one, which agrees with the proof.

hints.text: Before testing onto and one-to-one, ask whether $F$ even gives one value for each class. What could go wrong when a class has several names?
A rule defined on equivalence classes through a representative is well-defined only if it does not depend on which representative you pick.
For injectivity, assume two classes have the same image and show the classes coincide. For surjectivity, start from a target value and find a class that maps to it.
Translate "$[x] = [y]$" into a statement about $f(x)$ and $f(y)$, then use the definition of $\sim$ in both directions.
Pick an arbitrary $b \in B$ and use the fact that $f$ is onto to produce an element $a$ with $f(a) = b$. See what $F$ does to $[a]$.

variation.stem: Let $A = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, $B = \{p, q, r\}$ and let $f : A \to B$ be onto with $f(1) = f(2) = f(3) = p$, $f(4) = f(5) = q$, $f(6) = r$. Define $a_1 \sim a_2$ if $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$, let $\mathcal{E}$ be the set of classes, and define $F([x]) = f(x)$. Which of the following is/are TRUE?
variation.explanation: The classes are the fibres $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{4,5\}$ and $\{6\}$, so $\mathcal{E}$ has 3 elements and the first statement is false. $F$ sends these to $p$, $q$, $r$, which are distinct and cover $B$, so $F$ is one-to-one and onto.

questions.stem: Let $X$ be a set and $2^X$ denote the powerset of $X$. Define a binary operation $\Delta$ on $2^X$ as follows: $A \Delta B = (A - B) \cup (B - A)$. Let $H = (2^X, \Delta)$. Which of the following statements about $H$ is/are correct?
options: Every element in $H$ has an inverse, but $H$ is NOT a group.
For every $A \in 2^X$, the inverse of $A$ is the complement of $A$.
For every $A \in 2^X$, the inverse of $A$ is $A$.

solutionDiagram.alt: Operation table of the symmetric difference on the four subsets of {a, b}: the first row and column reproduce the headings, so the empty set is the identity, and every entry on the shaded diagonal is the empty set, so each set is its own inverse.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: The **powerset** $2^X$ is the set of all subsets of $X$. $A - B$ keeps the elements of $A$ that are not in $B$, so $A \Delta B$ keeps the elements that lie in exactly one of the two sets. A **group** is a set with an operation that is (1) closed, (2) associative, (3) has an identity $e$ with $A \Delta e = A$, and (4) gives every element an inverse $A'$ with $A \Delta A' = e$. The rule: check the four properties one by one.

steps.title: Closed, identity, inverse
steps.body: The result of $\Delta$ is a subset of $X$, so it is closed. $A \Delta \varnothing = A \cup \varnothing$ with nothing removed, so $\varnothing$ is the identity. And $A \Delta A = (A - A) \cup (A - A) = \varnothing$, so every set is its own inverse.

steps.title: Associativity
steps.body: An element $x$ belongs to $A \Delta B$ exactly when it lies in exactly one of $A$ and $B$, so the number of sets among $A, B$ that contain $x$ is odd (1 rather than 0 or 2). Applying this twice, $x \in (A \Delta B) \Delta C$ exactly when the number of sets among $A, B, C$ that contain $x$ is odd. The same holds for $A \Delta (B \Delta C)$. So both groupings give the same set, and $\Delta$ is associative.

steps.title: Read off the options
steps.body: All four group properties hold, so A is true and B is false. The inverse of $A$ is $A$, so D is true. C is false: the complement of $A$ would need $A \Delta A^c = \varnothing$, but $A \Delta A^c = X$; for $A = \varnothing$ the complement is $X$ and $\varnothing \Delta X = X \ne \varnothing$. A brute-force check on all subsets of a 3-element set confirms associativity, the identity $\varnothing$, inverse equal to the set itself, and that the complement is not the inverse. The answer is A and D.

shortcut.body: Think of a subset as a row of membership bits. $\Delta$ is bit-by-bit XOR: associative, with identity all zeros, and $x \oplus x = 0$. So $H$ is a group in which every element is its own inverse: A and D. A minute.

traps.text: Option B treats "every element has an inverse" as a separate property from being a group. It is one of the four group axioms, and $\Delta$ also satisfies the other three.
Option C confuses $\Delta$ with the Boolean complement of lattice thinking. $A \Delta A^c = X$, which is not the identity $\varnothing$.
Doubting A because associativity of $\Delta$ is not obvious from the formula. The odd-membership argument (or the XOR view) proves it in one line.

recognize.clues: A binary operation is defined on a family of sets and the options ask whether it forms a group and what the inverse of an element is. That is a group-axiom check.
recognize.contrast: The complement is the natural guess for an inverse because it works for union and intersection in a Boolean algebra. Here the operation is symmetric difference, so test the identity equation $A \Delta A' = e$ and not the Boolean intuition.

check.body: Substitute into a small case. For $X = \{1, 2\}$ the four subsets under $\Delta$ give $\{1\} \Delta \{2\} = \{1,2\}$, and every subset combined with itself gives $\varnothing$. The table is that of the Klein four-group, where every element is its own inverse. The complement of $\{1\}$ is $\{2\}$, and $\{1\} \Delta \{2\} \ne \varnothing$.

A group needs four things: closure, associativity, an identity, and an inverse for every element.

Describe each subset by a row of membership bits, one per element of $X$. See what $\Delta$ does to a single position.

variation.stem: Let $X = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and let $H = (2^X, \cup)$, the subsets of $X$ with union as the operation. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: Every element of $H$ has an inverse in $H$.
variation.explanation: Union is closed and associative, and $A \cup \varnothing = A$, so $\varnothing$ is the identity. An inverse of $A$ would need $A \cup A' = \varnothing$, which forces $A = \varnothing$. So only $\varnothing$ has an inverse and $H$ is not a group.

questions.stem: Let $G$ be a simple, finite, undirected graph with vertex set $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$. Let $\Delta(G)$ denote the maximum degree of $G$ and let $N = \{1, 2, \ldots\}$ denote the set of all possible colors. Color the vertices of $G$ using the following greedy strategy:

code.text:
for i = 1, ..., n
    color(v_i) <- min{ j in N : no neighbour of v_i is colored j }

options: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of $G$.
The number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G) + 1$.
The number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G)$.
The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of $G$.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: a path p1 - p2 - p3 - p4 processed in the order p4, p3, p1, p2 receives colours 1, 3, 2, 1 from left to right, using three colours though two suffice. Right: a triangle coloured 1, 2, 3, which uses three colours although its maximum degree is 2.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A colouring is **proper** when adjacent vertices have different colours. The **degree** of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and $\Delta(G)$ is the largest degree in the graph. The **chromatic number** is the fewest colours any proper colouring needs. The greedy strategy visits the vertices in the given order and gives each the smallest colour that none of its already-coloured neighbours uses. The key fact: when $v_i$ is coloured, at most $\deg(v_i)$ colours are blocked, so one of the colours $1, 2, \dots, \deg(v_i) + 1$ is free.

steps.title: A is true: the colouring is proper
steps.body: When $v_i$ picks its colour it avoids every neighbour that is already coloured. A neighbour coloured later does the same and avoids $v_i$'s colour. So for every edge, whichever end is coloured second differs from the first.

steps.title: B is true: at most Δ + 1 colours
steps.body: At most $\deg(v_i) \le \Delta(G)$ colours are blocked for $v_i$, so the smallest free colour is at most $\Delta(G) + 1$. No vertex receives a larger colour, so the number of colours used is at most $\Delta(G) + 1$.

steps.title: C and D are false
steps.body: For C take the triangle $K_3$: $\Delta = 2$, but its three vertices pairwise adjacent force the colours 1, 2, 3, so 3 colours are used. For D the order matters. On the path $p_1 - p_2 - p_3 - p_4$ process $p_4, p_3, p_1, p_2$: $p_4$ gets 1, $p_3$ gets 2, $p_1$ gets 1, and $p_2$ sees colours 1 and 2 and takes 3. Three colours are used, but the path is bipartite and 2 colours suffice. An exhaustive check over every graph on up to 6 vertices and every vertex order confirms A and B always hold and C and D can fail. The answer is A and B.

shortcut.body: A and B are the two standard facts about greedy colouring (proper, and at most $\Delta + 1$ colours). Kill C with a triangle ($\Delta = 2$, 3 colours) and D by remembering that greedy depends on the vertex order. A minute and a half.

traps.text: Option C is Brooks' theorem, which says $\chi \le \Delta$ for connected graphs that are neither complete nor an odd cycle, and which is about the best colouring, not the greedy one. The triangle needs $\Delta + 1 = 3$.
Option D assumes greedy is optimal. It is optimal for some vertex orders only; a bad order on a 4-vertex path uses 3 colours where 2 suffice.

recognize.clues: The stem describes a greedy colouring procedure and the options bound the number of colours by $\Delta(G)$ and by the chromatic number. That points to the greedy colouring bounds.
recognize.contrast: The chromatic number is the minimum over all proper colourings. Greedy gives one particular colouring that depends on the vertex order, so it only gives an upper bound and need not match the minimum.

check.body: Test the bound on the complete graph $K_4$. Here $\Delta = 3$, and any order forces four distinct colours, so greedy uses $\Delta + 1 = 4$. The bound $\Delta + 1$ is reached, which shows the weaker bound $\Delta$ cannot hold in general.

variation.stem: Colour the vertices of the 5-cycle $v_1 v_2 v_3 v_4 v_5$ (with $v_5$ adjacent to $v_1$) greedily in the order $v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4, v_5$, giving each vertex the smallest colour in $\{1, 2, \ldots\}$ not used by an already-coloured neighbour. Which of the following is/are TRUE?
options: Some vertex order makes greedy use 4 colours on this graph.
variation.explanation: Colours go 1, 2, 1, 2 for $v_1$ to $v_4$, and $v_5$ sees both 1 (from $v_1$) and 2 (from $v_4$), so it takes 3. The colouring is proper and uses 3 colours. Since $\Delta = 2$ no order can use more than $\Delta + 1 = 3$ colours, so the last statement is false.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for a group $G$?
options: If for all $x, y \in G$, $(xy)^2 = x^2y^2$, then $G$ is commutative.
If for all $x \in G$, $x^2 = 1$, then $G$ is commutative. Here, 1 is the identity element of $G$.
If the order of $G$ is 2, then $G$ is commutative.
If $G$ is commutative, then a subgroup of $G$ need not be commutative.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A **group** is a set with an associative operation, an identity element $1$, and an inverse $x^{-1}$ for every $x$. It is **commutative** when $xy = yx$ for all $x, y$. The **order** of $G$ is its number of elements. A **subgroup** is a subset that is a group under the same operation. The working rule in a group is cancellation: from $ax = ay$ multiply by $a^{-1}$ on the left to get $x = y$, and from $xb = yb$ multiply by $b^{-1}$ on the right.

steps.title: A is true
steps.body: $(xy)^2 = xyxy$ and $x^2y^2 = xxyy$. If they are equal, cancel $x$ on the left and $y$ on the right of $xyxy = xxyy$ to get $yx = xy$. So the condition for all $x, y$ is exactly commutativity.

steps.title: B is true
steps.body: If $x^2 = 1$ for every $x$, then every element is its own inverse: $x^{-1} = x$. For any $x, y$ the product $xy$ is also an element, so $xy = (xy)^{-1} = y^{-1}x^{-1} = yx$.

steps.title: C is true and D is false
steps.body: A group of order 2 is $\{1, g\}$. The identity commutes with everything, and $g$ commutes with itself, so every pair commutes: C is true. For D: any two elements of a subgroup are also elements of $G$, and in a commutative group any two elements commute, so the subgroup is commutative too. "Need not be" is false. The answer is A, B and C. A check over all subgroups of the permutations of 4 objects generated by one or two elements found no group where A, B or C fail.

shortcut.body: A: expand $(xy)^2$ and cancel to $yx = xy$. B: $x^{-1} = x$, then $xy = (xy)^{-1} = yx$. C: only two elements. D: a subgroup inherits commutativity, since the property is about pairs of elements. About 20 seconds each, a minute in all.

traps.text: Rejecting A because $(xy)^2 \ne x^2y^2$ in general. In a non-commutative group it fails for some pair, but the statement asks for equality for all pairs, and that forces commutativity.

Rejecting B because squares equal to 1 looks like a weak condition. It is strong: it forces every element to be its own inverse, and the product trick then gives commutativity (such groups are the elementary abelian 2-groups).
Choosing D because subgroups sometimes behave differently from the whole group (for example, normality). Commutativity is a statement about pairs of elements, and a subgroup only has fewer pairs.

recognize.clues: Each option states a condition on a group and asks about commutativity or subgroups. That is a group-theory proof exercise with the axioms and cancellation as the tools.
recognize.contrast: These are statements about all groups, so a condition that holds in many familiar examples is not enough. Do not assume commutativity when expanding $(xy)^2$.

check.body: Test against the smallest non-commutative group, the permutations of 3 objects. It contains a transposition pair $x, y$ with $x^2 = y^2 = 1$ but $(xy)^2 \ne 1$, so the hypotheses of the first two statements fail there, as they must for a group that is not commutative. Every group of order 2 is $\{1, g\}$, which is commutative.

variation.stem: Consider a group $G$. Which of the following claims is/are always true?
options: If $x^3 = 1$ for every $x \in G$, then $G$ is commutative.
If $(xy)^{-1} = x^{-1}y^{-1}$ for all $x, y \in G$, then $G$ is commutative.
variation.explanation: A group of order 3 has only the identity and two other elements, one the square of the other, so it is commutative. questions.stem: Consider a simple undirected graph of 10 vertices. If the graph is disconnected, then the maximum number of edges it can have is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The complete graph on 9 vertices drawn with all 36 edges, next to one isolated vertex, and a table of edge counts for splits of 10 vertices into parts of sizes 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5, giving 36, 29, 24, 21 and 20.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A graph is **simple** when it has no loops and no repeated edges, so two vertices share at most one edge. It is **disconnected** when its vertices split into at least two groups with no edge between the groups. A **complete graph** $K_m$ has every pair of its $m$ vertices joined, so it has $\binom{m}{2} = m(m-1)/2$ edges. The rule: a disconnected graph on 10 vertices lies inside two groups of sizes $a$ and $10 - a$ with no edge between them, and the most edges come from filling each group completely.

steps.title: Count edges for each split
steps.body: With sides of sizes $a$ and $10 - a$, the edge count is at most the sum of the two complete graphs. For $a = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ this gives 36, 29, 24, 21, 20.

steps.title: Pick the maximum
steps.body: The count falls as the split gets more even, so it is largest at $a = 1$: a single isolated vertex and a complete graph on the other 9 vertices. That graph has $\binom{9}{2} = 36$ edges. Brute force over all graphs on 2 to 6 vertices confirms the maximum is $\binom{n-1}{2}$.

shortcut.body: For $n$ vertices the maximum is $\binom{n-1}{2}$: a complete graph on $n - 1$ vertices plus one isolated vertex. With $n = 10$ that is $\binom{9}{2} = 36$. Equivalent: $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ pairs, minus the 9 pairs that touch the isolated vertex, is 36.

traps.text: 45 is $\binom{10}{2}$, the complete graph on all 10 vertices, which is connected.
44 comes from deleting a single edge from $K_{10}$. The graph is still connected, so it does not satisfy the condition.
20 comes from splitting into two equal halves of 5, which gives the fewest edges among the splits, not the most.

recognize.clues: The words "disconnected", "simple" and "maximum number of edges" together signal that the extremal graph is a complete graph on most vertices plus the smallest possible separate part.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with the minimum edges needed for a graph to be connected, which is a tree with $n - 1$ edges. The maximum without connectivity is a different, much larger count.

check.body: Second route by missing edges. A simple graph on 10 vertices has at most 45 edges, and the complete graph is connected. A candidate with 36 edges is missing exactly the 9 edges at one vertex, and adding any one of them reconnects the graph. Any graph with more than 36 edges is missing at most 8 pairs, which is too few to cut a vertex or a group off from the rest.

questions.stem: The number of arrangements of six identical balls in three identical bins is______.

solutionDiagram.alt: The seven ways to put six identical balls into three identical bins, drawn as three boxes per row with dots for balls: 6-0-0, 5-1-0, 4-2-0, 4-1-1, 3-3-0, 3-2-1 and 2-2-2.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: Balls that are **identical** cannot be told apart, so swapping two balls changes nothing: all that matters is how many balls each bin holds. Bins that are **identical** cannot be told apart either, so the arrangement with 6 balls in the first bin equals the arrangement with 6 balls in the second. An arrangement is therefore just a collection of three numbers, each at least 0, adding up to 6, with no order among them. Such a collection is a **partition of 6 into at most 3 parts**. The rule: list the numbers from largest to smallest, so that each arrangement appears exactly once.

steps.title: List by the largest bin
steps.body: Write the bins as $x \ge y \ge z \ge 0$ with $x + y + z = 6$. Largest bin 6: (6,0,0). Largest 5: (5,1,0). Largest 4: (4,2,0) and (4,1,1). Largest 3: (3,3,0) and (3,2,1). Largest 2: (2,2,2). A largest bin of 1 or less cannot reach 6 with three bins.

steps.title: Count and confirm
steps.body: There are 7 arrangements. Enumerating all triples of non-negative numbers summing to 6 and keeping each unordered multiset once also gives 7.

shortcut.body: The number 6 has 11 partitions in all. Those with more than 3 parts are $3+1+1+1$, $2+2+1+1$, $2+1+1+1+1$ and $1+1+1+1+1+1$: 4 of them. So $11 - 4 = 7$. If the partitions are not memorised, the list by largest bin takes about 2 minutes.

traps.text: 28 is $\binom{8}{2}$, the stars-and-bars count for identical balls in distinguishable bins. The bins here are identical, so many of those 28 are the same arrangement.
11 is the number of partitions of 6 with any number of parts. Only three bins exist, so partitions with 4 or more parts are not allowed.
729 is $3^6$, which treats the balls as distinguishable and assigns each ball a bin.

recognize.clues: "Identical balls" and "identical bins" together mean neither the items nor the containers carry labels, so the count is of partitions into at most 3 parts, not of placements.
recognize.contrast: If the bins were distinct, the count would be a stars-and-bars binomial coefficient. Identical bins collapse that count, because arrangements that differ only by swapping bins are the same.

check.body: Cross-check with the distinct-bins count. Six identical balls in three distinct bins can be placed in $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ ways. Group those by sorted size: the sorted patterns with three different sizes count 6 ways each, with exactly two equal sizes 3 ways each, and all equal 1 way. With three patterns of the first kind ($3 \cdot 6 = 18$), three of the second ($3 \cdot 3 = 9$) and one of the third ($1$), the total is $18 + 9 + 1 = 28$, so there are $3 + 3 + 1 = 7$ patterns.

questions.stem:
Which one of the following is the closed form for the generating function of the sequence $\{a_n\}_{n \ge 0}$ defined below?

$$a_n = \begin{cases} n + 1, & n \text{ is odd} \\ 1, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: The **generating function** of a sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ is the power series $G(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^n$, with the sequence stored as coefficients. A **closed form** is a fraction that expands to that series. Two basic series do most of the work: $\sum_{n \ge 0} x^n = \frac{1}{1-x}$, and $x\frac{d}{dx}$ applied to a series multiplies the coefficient of $x^n$ by $n$. The rule: split $a_n$ into pieces whose series are known and add them.

steps.title: Split the sequence
steps.body: For even $n$ the term is 1. For odd $n$ it is $n + 1 = 1 + n$. So $a_n$ is 1 for every $n$, plus an extra $n$ when $n$ is odd. The series is therefore the all-ones series plus the series of $n x^n$ over odd $n$.

steps.title: Series of n over odd n
steps.body: The odd powers alone sum to $x + x^3 + x^5 + \cdots = \frac{x}{1-x^2}$. Applying $x\frac{d}{dx}$ multiplies each coefficient by its exponent $n$. By the quotient rule, $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{1-x^2} = \frac{(1-x^2) + 2x^2}{(1-x^2)^2} = \frac{1+x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}$, so the series is $\frac{x(1+x^2)}{(1-x^2)^2}$.

steps.title: Add and match
steps.body: Adding the two parts gives option A. Expanding each option as a series confirms it: A gives $1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 6, 1, 8, \dots$, which is $a_n$; B gives $1, 4, 1, 6, \dots$; C gives $1, 3, 1, 5, \dots$; D gives $1, 2, 1, 3, \dots$.

shortcut.body: Compute the first odd terms: $a_1 = 2$ and $a_3 = 4$. Expanding with $\frac{1}{(1-x^2)^2} = 1 + 2x^2 + \cdots$, the coefficient of $x$ in each option is: A $1 + 1 = 2$, B $3 + 1 = 4$, C $2 + 1 = 3$, D $1 + 1 = 2$. That removes B and C. For $x^3$: A gives $3 + 1 = 4$ and D gives $2 + 1 = 3$. Only A matches. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Option B has coefficients $n + 3$ on odd $n$. Its fraction $\frac{x(3-x^2)}{(1-x^2)^2} = 3x + 5x^3 + 7x^5 + \cdots$ already gives $n + 2$ at odd $n$, and $\frac{1}{1-x}$ adds another 1, so the odd terms are 2 too large (4 instead of 2 at $n = 1$).

Option C uses $\frac{2x}{(1-x^2)^2} = \sum (n+1)x^n$ over odd $n$, which is correct for the odd places. Then it must be completed with $\frac{1}{1-x^2}$ (even places only), not $\frac{1}{1-x}$, which also adds 1 at the odd places.
Option D uses $\frac{x}{(1-x^2)^2} = \sum \frac{n+1}{2}x^n$ over odd $n$, half of the required coefficient: $\sum_{k \ge 0}(k+1)x^{2k+1}$ has $k + 1 = (n+1)/2$.

recognize.clues: The sequence is given by a rule that changes with the parity of $n$, and the options are closed forms with $\frac{1}{1-x}$ and $(1-x^2)^2$ in the denominators. That is the signal to split by parity and use known series.
recognize.contrast: Do not use the same closed form for both parities. A formula valid only on odd or only on even indices must be built from a series in $x^2$, not in $x$.

check.body: Numerical check at $x = 1/2$. Summing $a_n x^n$ over many terms of the sequence gives $28/9 \approx 3.1111$, and option A evaluates to the same value, while B, C and D give $4.4444$, $3.7778$ and $2.8889$. The test needs no expansion beyond a calculator.

variation.stem: Which one of the following is the closed form for the generating function of the sequence $\{a_n\}_{n \ge 0}$ given by $a_n = n + 1$ if $n$ is even and $a_n = 1$ otherwise?
variation.explanation: Write $a_n = 1 + n$ on even $n$ and $1$ on odd $n$, so the sequence is the all-ones series plus the series of $n x^n$ over even $n$. The even powers sum to $\frac{1}{1-x^2}$, and $x\frac{d}{dx}$ turns that into $\frac{2x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}$. questions.stem: Consider a simple undirected unweighted graph with at least three vertices. If $A$ is the adjacency matrix of the graph, then the number of 3-cycles in the graph is given by the trace of

solutionDiagram.alt: A triangle on vertices a, b, c with the six closed walks of length 3 listed: abca, acba, bcab, bacb, cabc, cbac. The trace of A cubed is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, so the number of triangles is the trace divided by 6.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: The **adjacency matrix** $A$ has $A[i][j] = 1$ when vertices $i$ and $j$ are joined by an edge and 0 otherwise; for a simple undirected graph it is symmetric with zeros on the diagonal. A **3-cycle** (triangle) is three vertices that are pairwise adjacent. The key fact: the entry $A^k[i][j]$ counts the **walks** of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$, where a walk may revisit vertices. The **trace** is the sum of the diagonal entries, so $\operatorname{tr}(A^3)$ counts closed walks of length 3, walks that return to their starting vertex.

steps.title: What a closed walk of length 3 is
steps.body: A closed walk $i \to j \to k \to i$ has three steps along edges. There are no loops, so $i, j, k$ are consecutive different vertices, and $k$ is adjacent to $i$ as well: $i, j, k$ are pairwise adjacent and form a triangle. So every closed 3-walk lies on a triangle.

steps.title: Count the walks per triangle
steps.body: One triangle with vertices $a, b, c$ yields closed 3-walks by choosing the start vertex (3 ways) and the direction around the triangle (2 ways): $3 \times 2 = 6$ walks, listed in the figure. Hence the trace is 6 times the number of triangles, and the number of triangles is the trace divided by 6. For $K_3$, $A^3$ has diagonal entries 2, 2, 2, trace 6, one triangle. A check over every graph on 3 to 6 vertices confirms $\operatorname{tr}(A^3) = 6 \times (\text{triangles})$.

shortcut.body: Take $K_3$: one triangle, $A^3$ has trace $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$. So divide by 6. Thirty seconds, and the single example separates the four options.

traps.text: The trace of $A^3$ alone counts closed walks, not triangles. Each triangle is counted six times.
Dividing by 2 corrects only for direction (two ways around the triangle) and forgets that each of the 3 starting vertices gives its own walk.
Dividing by 3 corrects only for the starting vertex and forgets that the two directions around the triangle are different walks.

recognize.clues: The phrases "adjacency matrix", "trace" and "number of 3-cycles" together point to counting closed walks of length 3, because powers of $A$ count walks and the trace picks out the closed ones.
recognize.contrast: A closed walk is not a cycle: the trace counts every walk that returns to its start, so a cycle is counted once for each start vertex and each direction. Compare with $\sum_{i,j} A[i][j]$, which counts each edge twice for the same reason.

check.body: Second route on $K_4$: from a fixed vertex step to one of 3 neighbours, then to one of the 2 vertices that are neither the start nor the current vertex, then return. That is 6 closed walks per vertex, so the trace is 24, while $K_4$ has $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ triangles. The ratio is the same 6 per triangle as for $K_3$.

Powers of an adjacency matrix count walks: $A^k[i][j]$ is the number of walks of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$, and a walk may revisit vertices and edges.

In a simple graph a closed walk of length 3 has no loop to hide in, so it must run round a triangle. The trace therefore counts triangles with a multiplicity, and the work is finding that multiplicity.
Fix one triangle on vertices $a, b, c$ and list every closed walk of length 3 on it. Decide what you vary (where the walk starts, which way it goes round) and count the combinations.

variation.stem: Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of the complete graph $K_5$ on five vertices. The value of $\operatorname{tr}(A^3)$ is
variation.explanation: $\operatorname{tr}(A^3)$ counts closed walks of length 3, and each triangle gives $3 \times 2 = 6$ of them (3 starting vertices, 2 directions). $K_5$ has $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ triangles, so the trace is $60$. questions.stem: The following simple undirected graph is referred to as the Peterson graph. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.figure: Figure 1 (the given graph): ten vertices. Five outer vertices $a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$ are the corners of a pentagon, $a_0$ at the top and the others clockwise, joined in the cycle $a_0a_1a_2a_3a_4a_0$. Five inner vertices $b_0, \dots, b_4$ lie inside, $b_i$ on the same side as $a_i$ and joined to it by a spoke $a_ib_i$. The inner vertices form a five-pointed star: $b_i$ is joined to $b_{i+2}$ (indices mod 5), giving $b_0b_2$, $b_2b_4$, $b_4b_1$, $b_1b_3$, $b_3b_0$. Total 15 edges. Figure 2 (used in option C): nine vertices $c_0, \dots, c_8$ on a ring, $c_0$ at the top and the others clockwise, joined in the 9-cycle $c_0c_1\dots c_8c_0$; one centre vertex $z$ joined to $c_0$, $c_3$ and $c_6$; and three straight chords $c_1c_5$, $c_2c_7$ and $c_4c_8$. Total 15 edges.

diagram.alt: Left: the Peterson graph drawn as an outer pentagon a0 to a4, an inner five-pointed star b0 to b4 and five spokes. Right: the graph of option C, a nine-sided ring c0 to c8 with a centre vertex z joined to c0, c3 and c6 and three chords c1c5, c2c7 and c4c8.

options: The chromatic number of the graph is 3.
The graph has a Hamiltonian path.
The following graph is isomorphic to the Peterson graph.
The size of the largest independent set of the given graph is 3. (A subset of vertices of a graph form an independent set if no two vertices of the subset are adjacent.)

solutionDiagram.alt: Three copies of the Peterson graph. Left: a proper colouring with numbers 1, 2, 3 on the vertices. Middle: a Hamiltonian path drawn in bold and numbered 1 to 10 along the path. Right: the nine-ring graph of option C relabelled with the Peterson names a0 to a4 and b0 to b4, showing that every edge matches.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A proper **colouring** gives different colours to adjacent vertices, and the **chromatic number** is the fewest colours needed. A **Hamiltonian path** visits every vertex exactly once, moving along edges. An **independent set** is a set of vertices no two of which are adjacent. Two graphs are **isomorphic** when the vertices of one can be renamed as the vertices of the other so that edges go to edges and non-edges to non-edges. The Peterson graph has 10 vertices, every vertex of degree 3, and 15 edges. The rule: for each statement find a witness (a colouring, a path, a renaming, an independent set) or prove none exists.

steps.title: A is true: three colours
steps.body: The outer cycle $a_0a_1a_2a_3a_4$ is an odd cycle, and an odd cycle cannot be coloured with 2 colours (the colours would have to alternate around it), so at least 3 are needed. The colouring in the figure uses exactly 3, with no two adjacent vertices sharing a number. So the chromatic number is 3.

steps.title: B is true: a path through all ten vertices
steps.body: Take the walk below. Each consecutive pair is an edge: $a_0a_1$, $a_1a_2$, $a_2a_3$, $a_3a_4$ are outer edges, $a_4b_4$ is a spoke, and $b_4b_2$, $b_2b_0$, $b_0b_3$, $b_3b_1$ are star edges. All ten vertices occur once. The Peterson graph has no Hamiltonian cycle, but the question asks only for a path.

steps.title: C is true: rename the ring graph
steps.body: Rename the vertices of Figure 2 as $c_0 \to a_0$, $c_1 \to a_1$, $c_2 \to a_2$, $c_3 \to a_3$, $c_4 \to b_3$, $c_5 \to b_1$, $c_6 \to b_4$, $c_7 \to b_2$, $c_8 \to b_0$ and $z \to a_4$. The ring edges $c_0c_1, c_1c_2, c_2c_3$ become outer edges, $c_3c_4$ becomes the spoke $a_3b_3$, $c_4c_5, c_5c_6, c_6c_7, c_7c_8$ become star edges $b_3b_1, b_1b_4, b_4b_2, b_2b_0$, and $c_8c_0$ becomes the spoke $b_0a_0$. The spokes of $z$ become $a_4a_0, a_4a_3, a_4b_4$, and the chords become $a_1b_1, a_2b_2, b_0b_3$. All 15 edges land on Peterson edges, and the map is one-to-one, so the graphs are isomorphic. A search over all renamings finds this one.

steps.title: D is false: an independent set of size 4
steps.body: The vertices $a_1, a_3, b_0, b_4$ are pairwise non-adjacent (the figure's colour class of four). So an independent set of size 4 exists and the largest is not 3. The colouring bound explains why: 10 vertices in 3 colour classes means some class has at least $\lceil 10/3 \rceil = 4$ vertices. The answer is A, B and C.

shortcut.body: Know the Peterson graph's profile: chromatic number 3, largest independent set 4, a Hamiltonian path but no Hamiltonian cycle, 3-regular on 10 vertices with shortest cycle 5. A, B and D follow from that. For C count degrees (all 3) and edges (15) and check that the graph has no triangle or 4-cycle: a cubic graph on 10 vertices with shortest cycle 5 is the Peterson graph. About 3 minutes.

traps.text: Believing the chromatic number is 4 or 2. An odd cycle forces at least 3, and 3 colours are enough, so the value is exactly 3.
Confusing a Hamiltonian path with a Hamiltonian cycle. The Peterson graph famously has no Hamiltonian cycle, but it has a path through all ten vertices.
Dismissing C because the drawing looks nothing like the pentagon-and-star picture. A drawing says nothing about isomorphism; compare degrees, cycle lengths and edge by edge.
Taking the largest independent set to be 3 because the chromatic number is 3. With 3 colours on 10 vertices some colour is used at least 4 times, and a colour class is independent.

recognize.clues: A named graph shown only as a drawing, with four separate claims (chromatic number, Hamiltonian path, isomorphism to a second drawing, largest independent set), points to a witness-or-obstruction check per option using degrees, cycle lengths and counting.
recognize.contrast: A Hamiltonian path is not a Hamiltonian cycle, and this graph is the standard example that separates them. A different-looking drawing says nothing about isomorphism: compare degree and cycle structure, then match edge by edge.

check.body: Test the explicit set $\{a_1, a_3, b_0, b_4\}$ against the edge list. The neighbours are $a_1$: $a_0, a_2, b_1$; $a_3$: $a_2, a_4, b_3$; $b_0$: $a_0, b_2, b_3$; $b_4$: $a_4, b_1, b_2$. None of the four appears in another's list, so the set is independent and has size 4.

Recall what each word asks for: a proper colouring, a Hamiltonian path, an isomorphism and an independent set. Some are settled by showing one example, others need a reason why no example exists.
Isomorphism preserves degrees, the edge count and cycle lengths, so any mismatch rules it out, and when all agree only an explicit renaming proves it. A drawing that looks different proves nothing.

variation.stem: Consider the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$: two groups of three vertices, with every vertex joined to all three vertices of the other group and to nothing in its own group. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The chromatic number of the graph is 2.
The graph has a Hamiltonian cycle.
The size of the largest independent set of the graph is 2.
The graph has a perfect matching, a set of 3 edges that share no vertex.
variation.explanation: Every edge joins the two groups, so two colours suffice and one does not (the graph has an edge). Walking alternately between the groups visits all six vertices and returns, so a Hamiltonian cycle exists. Each group is an independent set of size 3, so the largest independent set is not 2. Pairing the $i$-th vertex of one group with the $i$-th of the other gives a perfect matching. The true options are A, B and D, confirmed by enumeration.

questions.stem:
Consider the following recurrence:

$$f(1) = 1;$$
$$f(2n) = 2f(n) - 1, \quad \text{for } n \ge 1;$$
$$f(2n+1) = 2f(n) + 1, \quad \text{for } n \ge 1.$$

Then, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: Bar chart of f(n) for n from 1 to 16: the values are 1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 5, 7, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 1. The bars at powers of 2 are shaded and equal 1, and between them the values climb by 2.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: A **recurrence** defines $f(m)$ from $f$ at smaller arguments. Here $f(m)$ comes from $f(\lfloor m/2 \rfloor)$: even $m = 2n$ gives $2f(n) - 1$ and odd $m = 2n + 1$ gives $2f(n) + 1$, ending at $f(1) = 1$. A statement "true" means it holds for every $n$ allowed. The rule: compute a table of small values, spot the pattern, prove it by induction, then test each option against the pattern.

steps.title: Prove the pattern
steps.body: Claim: for $0 \le r < 2^k$, $f(2^k + r) = 2r + 1$. It holds for $k = 0$ ($f(1) = 1$). Suppose it holds for $m = 2^k + r$. Then $f(2m) = 2f(m) - 1 = 2(2r + 1) - 1 = 4r + 1$, and $2m = 2^{k+1} + 2r$ so the claim needs $2(2r) + 1 = 4r + 1$. Also $f(2m + 1) = 2(2r + 1) + 1 = 4r + 3$, and $2m + 1 = 2^{k+1} + (2r + 1)$ needs $2(2r + 1) + 1 = 4r + 3$. Both match, so the claim holds for all $m$.

steps.title: Test the four options
steps.body: A: $2^n - 1 = 2^{n-1} + (2^{n-1} - 1)$, so $r = 2^{n-1} - 1$ and $f = 2r + 1 = 2^n - 1$. True. B: $2^n = 2^n + 0$, so $f = 1$. True. C: $5 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+2} + 2^n$ with $2^n < 2^{n+2}$, so $r = 2^n$ and $f = 2^{n+1} + 1$. True. D: $2^n + 1$ has $r = 1$, so $f = 3$, and $3 \ne 2^n + 1$ once $n \ge 2$ (for example $f(5) = 3$, not 5). False. The answer is A, B and C; a script over $n$ up to 14 agrees.

shortcut.body: List $f(1)$ to $f(8)$: $1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 5, 7, 1$. A: $f(7) = 7$, B: $f(4) = 1$, C with $n = 1$: $f(10) = 2f(5) - 1 = 5 = 2^2 + 1$. D with $n = 2$: $f(5) = 3 \ne 5$. Spot checks cannot prove a statement for all $n$, but the pattern $f(2^k + r) = 2r + 1$ (which you can prove in one line) turns them into proofs.

traps.text: Option D is the natural analogue of A, but $2^n + 1$ sits just after a reset: $f(2^n + 1) = 2 \cdot 1 + 1 = 3$ for every $n \ge 1$, so it equals $2^n + 1$ only at $n = 1$.
Option C is dropped because the factor 5 looks unrelated to powers of 2. Write $5 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+2} + 2^n$ and the pattern gives the value.
Option A is true for all $n$, not only small ones: $2^n - 1$ is the last number before the next reset, where $r$ is as large as it can be and $f = 2r + 1$ reaches $2^n - 1$.

recognize.clues: Definitions of $f(2n)$ and $f(2n+1)$ in terms of $f(n)$, with options that substitute $2^n - 1$, $2^n$, $5 \cdot 2^n$ and $2^n + 1$, call for tabulating values and reading the binary shape of each argument.
recognize.contrast: This is not a linear recurrence with constant coefficients, so no characteristic equation applies. It also differs from the divide-and-conquer recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$, where the master theorem gives growth rates rather than exact values.

check.body: Test the pattern on a value outside the table. By the rule, $f(5) = 3$, then $f(10) = 2f(5) - 1 = 5$ and $f(21) = 2f(10) + 1 = 11$. Writing $21 = 16 + 5$, the pattern $f(2^k + r) = 2r + 1$ gives $2 \cdot 5 + 1 = 11$, the same value reached by two routes.

A recurrence that maps $n$ to $2n$ and $2n+1$ walks along the binary expansion of the argument, so think in binary.

A pattern read off a table is only a guess until induction confirms it: assume it for $m$ and check both $2m$ and $2m+1$. An option counts as true only if it holds for every allowed $n$, so one failing $n$ rejects it.
For each option write its argument as $2^k + r$ with $0 \le r < 2^k$. Work out $k$ and $r$ in terms of $n$, treating the pure powers of 2 as the case $r = 0$.
Compute $f(2) = 2f(1) - 1$ and $f(3) = 2f(1) + 1$ first. Then use $f(2)$ and $f(3)$ to obtain $f(4)$ through $f(7)$ the same way.

variation.stem: Consider the recurrence $g(1) = 1$, $g(2n) = g(n)$ and $g(2n+1) = g(n) + 1$ for $n \ge 1$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every integer $n \ge 1$?
variation.explanation: Doubling leaves $g$ unchanged and the odd step adds one, so $g(m)$ is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of $m$. Then $2^n - 1$ has $n$ ones, $3 \cdot 2^n$ has two ones and $2^n$ has one. But $2^n + 1$ has two ones, which equals $n$ only when $n = 2$, so B fails. A script over $n$ up to 16 agrees.

questions.stem: Which of the properties hold for the adjacency matrix $A$ of a simple undirected unweighted graph having $n$ vertices?
options: The diagonal entries of $A^2$ are the degrees of the vertices of the graph.
If the graph is connected, then none of the entries of $A^{n-1} + I_n$ can be zero.
If the sum of all the elements of $A$ is at most $2(n-1)$, then the graph must be acyclic.
If there is at least a 1 in each of $A$'s rows and columns, then the graph must be connected.

solutionDiagram.alt: Counterexamples: a path x - y - z for statement B, a triangle plus an isolated vertex for statement C, and two disjoint edges a-b and c-d for statement D.

steps.title: Definitions and the rule
steps.body: The **adjacency matrix** $A$ of a simple undirected graph has $A[i][j] = 1$ if $i$ and $j$ are adjacent and 0 otherwise; it is symmetric and has zeros on the diagonal. The **degree** of $i$ is its number of neighbours. A graph is **connected** when every two vertices are joined by a path, and **acyclic** when it has no cycle. The entry $A^k[i][j]$ counts walks of length $k$ from $i$ to $j$. The rule: prove a statement for every graph, or kill it with one small counterexample.

steps.title: A is true
steps.body: The diagonal entry of $A^2$ is $\sum_j A[i][j]\,A[j][i]$. By symmetry $A[j][i] = A[i][j]$, and a 0/1 entry squared is itself, so the sum is $\sum_j A[i][j]$: the number of neighbours of $i$, the degree.

steps.title: B is false
steps.body: Take the path $x - y - z$ with $n = 3$, a connected graph. Here $A^{n-1} = A^2$. A walk of length 2 from $x$ goes to $y$ and then to $x$ or $z$, never ending at $y$, so $A^2[x][y] = 0$, and the identity adds 0 off the diagonal. So $(A^2 + I)[x][y] = 0$. The true statement uses $(A + I)^{n-1}$, which has no zeros in a connected graph.

steps.title: C and D are false
steps.body: C: the sum of all entries of $A$ is twice the number of edges, so "at most $2(n-1)$" says at most $n - 1$ edges. Take a triangle plus an isolated vertex, $n = 4$: 3 edges, sum $6 = 2(n-1)$, but the triangle is a cycle. D: take two disjoint edges $a - b$ and $c - d$. Every row and column of $A$ has a 1, yet the graph is disconnected. A brute-force check over all graphs on 3 to 6 vertices found counterexamples to B, C and D and none to A. The answer is A.

shortcut.body: A is a one-line identity. For B, C and D draw the smallest counterexample: the 3-vertex path, a triangle plus an isolated vertex, and two disjoint edges. Under 3 minutes.

traps.text: Option B mixes up $A^{n-1} + I$ with $(A + I)^{n-1}$. The first can contain zeros: walks of a fixed length have fixed parity in a bipartite graph, so two vertices at odd distance get no walk of even length.
Option C assumes at most $n - 1$ edges means a tree. That holds only for connected graphs; with an isolated vertex the other vertices may use up all the edges on a cycle.
Option D takes "no isolated vertex" for connectivity. Two separate components, each with an edge, satisfy the condition without being connected.

recognize.clues: Claims about $A^2$, $A^{n-1} + I$, row sums and the total of all entries of $A$ point to walk counting and degree counting on a symmetric 0/1 matrix with a zero diagonal.
recognize.contrast: The expression $A^{n-1} + I$ is not $(A + I)^{n-1}$: only the second adds walks of every length up to $n - 1$, which is what a connectivity test needs. Check which of the two an option actually writes.

check.body: Test A and C on two other graphs. For A, take the path $x - y - z$: the diagonal of $A^2$ is $1, 2, 1$, the same as the degrees. For C, take a 4-cycle ($n = 4$): the entries of $A$ sum to $8 > 2(n-1) = 6$, so the premise fails and the claim says nothing, while the 3-vertex path has sum $4 = 2(n-1)$ and is acyclic, as C allows. Options B and D are settled by their counterexamples in the steps above.

hints.text: Four separate claims about adjacency matrices. Which can you prove for every graph, and which could a very small graph break?
